name: Emeka Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Emeka. I'm a field researcher from the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you say is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach PE and some Year 8 and 9 history at Castlegate School, a big secondary in an old factory town. My timetable's about half and half, so one hour I'm in the sports hall with a whistle and the next I'm explaining the causes of the First World War. I'm in at half seven to get the kit out, and on Wednesdays I run the after-school rugby. I like seeing a shy kid get picked for the team for the first time.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The history side, honestly, because I'm not a natural at the marking and the planning, and my head of department, Mr Ashworth, notices. I use the AI chatbot sometimes for history quiz questions, once I saw the others doing it. I live in a rented flat near my parents, I'm paying off a car loan, and I've got maybe three weeks of money saved. At weekends I coach the under-14s at the town rugby club, unpaid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's fine by me, schools should focus on getting kids fit and reading, not chasing gadgets. In the staffroom I'd probably joke that we can stop pretending the sports hall needs an app. I don't really post online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it changes very little. I teach PE in a sports hall with a leaking roof. No computer was ever going to fix the bucket under the basketball hoop. The history side might get slightly easier with the chatbot quizzes, and that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, get my history marking quicker with the chatbot quizzes, and keep running the Wednesday rugby. I'd ask Mr Ashworth if I could drop a history group next year and take more PE. And I'd pay an extra thirty a month off the car loan to finish it sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, mostly. It's not exciting, but I'm not worried about the job. The money's the only thing that nags.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Castlegate is in an old factory town. How does that shape things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lots of the kids' parents lost jobs when the tyre factory shut, my dad included, so people here don't trust big promises. That's partly why I'm in teaching, it felt like a job that couldn't be moved abroad. Castlegate is the main school in town, so it isn't going anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the money pressure, day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car loan, a hundred and ninety a month for another two years. Rent on the flat, which went up in September. I eat at my mum's twice a week, which helps more than I'd admit.

say: I'd say schools should focus on **fitness and reading**, not chasing gadgets.
I'd joke in the staffroom that the **sports hall** doesn't need an app.
think: I think the plateau **changes very little** for a PE teacher.
I think the **chatbot quizzes** make the history side slightly easier, and that's it.
do: Ask Mr Ashworth to **drop a history group** and take more PE.
Pay an extra **thirty a month** off the car loan.
feel: He feels **mostly settled**, with money the only nag.
S0.quote: I teach PE in a sports hall with a leaking roof. No computer was ever going to fix the bucket under the basketball hoop.
fieldNote: He feels his job is **secure** because Castlegate is the town's main school.
The real pressure is a **car loan** and rising rent on a thin cushion.
His father's **factory closure** shapes his distrust of big promises.

steps.text: Ask Mr Ashworth to swap a history group for more PE
Pay an extra thirty a month off the car loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine as long as the kids still get proper PE and proper teachers. At the rugby club I'd say the same, sport's the one thing a computer can't do for you. I'd use the tools once they're proven, same as everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's mostly the history side that changes. A machine can mark a history essay, but it can't stand on a muddy pitch in February and get fifteen lads to tackle properly. If the school needs fewer history teachers, I'd be happy to go full-time PE.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd learn the marking platform once Mr Ashworth's team picks one. I'd do my level two rugby coaching badge, which the club would part-fund. And I'd ask the head of PE, Mrs Kaur, if a full-time PE post might open up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not scared. I can see a way through, through the sports hall door. I just don't want to be the one left with the bits nobody wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your week is the kind of work on the card?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a third of it is planning, marking and reports for history. That's the bit that goes to the software. The rest is in the hall or on the pitch, and that stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Castlegate would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Ashworth, oddly, because his whole department is essays and marking. And the exams officer, Mrs Bell, who does all the booking and planning. She's been at Castlegate since my dad was at school there.

I'd use the tools **once proven**, same as everyone.
think: I think mostly the **history side** of my job changes.
I think I'd happily go **full-time PE** if history needed fewer teachers.
do: Learn the history **marking platform** once the department picks one.
Do the level two **rugby coaching** badge, part-funded by the club.
Ask Mrs Kaur about a **full-time PE** post.
feel: He feels **uneasy but not scared**, seeing a way through.
S1.quote: A machine can mark a history essay, but it can't stand on a muddy pitch in February and get fifteen lads to tackle properly.
fieldNote: He splits his own week clearly: a **third thinking work**, the rest hands-on.

He worries most about **office staff** and the history department, not himself.

steps.text: Learn the history marking platform once the department chooses one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and communities need to stick together, because nobody else is going to sort it in two years. At the rugby club I'd say keep the kids playing, whatever happens. I'd be wary of anyone promising the government will fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half my timetable is history and half is PE. The history half goes in 2028, and I'd have three years to make the PE half count. I'm not sure Castlegate can afford a full-time PE teacher if budgets get squeezed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd get the coaching badges done and ask about a full-time PE timetable straight away. I'd pick up paid holiday sports camps at the leisure centre for extra money. And I'd sell the car and buy something cheaper outright to kill the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd still have work, but maybe not all of it. Two years is quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2028, and robots for hands-on work around 2031. How does that split land for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The history marking, planning and explaining go in 2028. The PE, the refereeing, the first aid, the shouting from the touchline, that's hands-on, and robots for it wouldn't come till about 2031. So I'd have three years to become the PE and sport person and nothing else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the history hours went and no PE post opened, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be on part-time hours, maybe three days a week. I'd fill the rest with coaching and holiday camps, and I'd eat at my mum's more than twice a week. My family would help, they always do, but I'd hate needing it.

say: I'd say families and communities need to **stick together**.
I'd be wary of anyone promising **government** will fix it.
think: I think the **history half** of my timetable goes in 2028.
I think Castlegate may not afford a **full-time PE** teacher on tight budgets.
do: Finish **coaching badges** and ask for a full-time PE timetable straight away.
Run paid **holiday sports camps** at the leisure centre.
Sell the car and buy a **cheaper one outright** to clear the loan.
feel: He feels **anxious**, expecting to keep some work but maybe not all.
S2.quote: Half my timetable is history and half is PE. The history half goes in 2028, and I'd have three years to make the PE half count.
fieldNote: He maps the **thinking-first** timeline neatly onto his half-and-half timetable.
The risk is **part-time hours**, not losing the job outright.
He'd rely on **family** but dislikes needing it, fitting his traditional views.

steps.text: Ask the head for a full-time PE timetable
Run paid holiday sports camps at the leisure centre

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do it properly, and schools should keep sport and outdoor learning at the centre. At the club I'd say the same. I'd use the tools once they'd been tried, like always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's manageable. Five years is long enough to get my coaching badges and become the teacher the school can't do without on a Wednesday afternoon. The history side goes in 2031, but by then I'd want to be fully PE.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd take the level two badge, next year the level three, and I'd ask to run the Year 10 sports leadership course. I'd learn the AI planning tools for history while I still teach it. And I'd keep paying down the car loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. Not happy, but steady. I can see the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years buy you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three more years means I can get properly qualified and settled before any of it bites. The robots are 2034, which is a long way from a rugby pitch. It feels like enough time to do things right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You favour apprenticeships and family support. Would that shape what you'd tell your pupils?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd tell the lads to learn a trade or a skill with their hands as well as their heads. My dad's mates who retrained as electricians did all right. I'd want them ready, not waiting for handouts.

say: I'd say schools should keep **sport and outdoor** learning at the centre.
I'd use the tools **once tried**, like always.
think: I think it's **manageable**, as I'd be fully PE by 2031.
I think robots by **2034** are a long way from a rugby pitch.
do: Take level two then **level three** coaching badges over two years.
Ask to run the Year 10 **sports leadership** course.
Learn AI **planning tools** for history while still teaching it.
feel: He feels **steady**, not happy, but able to see the road.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to get my coaching badges and become the teacher the school can't do without on a Wednesday afternoon.
fieldNote: Five years lets him **sequence** coaching badges and a move into full-time PE.
He'd push pupils towards **trades and hands-on skills**, echoing his father's mates.
Thin savings and a car loan still keep him **uneasy**, not calm.

steps.text: Take level two and level three rugby coaching badges
Run the Year 10 sports leadership course
Use AI planning tools for his remaining history lessons

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so let's not panic, let's prepare. At the club I'd say the kids need sport more than ever. I wouldn't make a big deal of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it feels fine for me. My dad worked at the tyre factory for thirty years and retrained twice. Ten years of warning is more than he ever got. I'd be head of PE somewhere by then, if I work for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching both subjects for now and pick up AI tools for history as the department does. I'd get my coaching badges over the next few years without rushing. And I'd clear the car loan and start a proper savings pot, sixty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady. A bit uneasy about money, like always. Not worried about the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years out. Where are you by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Head of PE at Castlegate or the school in the next town. Maybe married, with a kid who hates rugby, knowing my luck. Still coaching on Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should be getting this right over the decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Families first, then employers, who should train people properly like the factory used to. Government should make sure schools keep sport and don't get sold nonsense. But mostly it's on us to get ready.

I'd tell the club kids need **sport** more than ever.
think: I think ten years is **more warning** than my dad ever got.
I think I could be **head of PE** by 2036 if I work for it.
do: Pick up **AI tools** for history as the department does.
Get **coaching badges** over the next few years without rushing.

fieldNote: He measures the decade against his **father's** two retrainings, and finds it generous.

steps.text: Keep teaching PE and history at Castlegate
Adopt AI tools for history when the department does

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my history hours would go before I'm qualified to fill them with PE. What would help is the school backing coaching qualifications, and keeping PE protected in the timetable. Not handouts, just a fair shot at the hands-on side.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: What it does to kids who already sit on screens all day. Kids don't learn to lose well from a screen. They learn it from a grown-up shaking the other team's hands first.

headlineQuote: Kids don't learn to lose well from a screen. They learn it from a grown-up shaking the other team's hands first.
portrait: Emeka is a 27-year-old teacher splitting his timetable between **PE and history** at a factory-town secondary.
He has a **car loan**, about three weeks of savings, and eats at his mum's twice a week.

He sees the **history half** of his job as exposed and plans to go fully PE.
He's **anxious** only when AGI comes in two years, and uneasy otherwise.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, when his **history hours** go before he can fill them with PE.
